inferno.1:
Dante is thirty-five, halfway through his life, when he finds himself lost in a dark forest. He does not know how he got there. He only knows he has left the right road.

At the edge of the forest he sees a hill with the morning sun on its top, and he starts to climb. But three wild animals block his way: a leopard, a lion, and a starving she-wolf. The wolf frightens him most, and she drives him back down into the dark.

There he meets a ghost. It is Virgil, a poet of ancient Rome and Dante's favorite writer. Virgil tells him he will never get past the wolf. He must take a longer road instead. Virgil will lead him down through Hell and up the mountain of Purgatory. After that another guide, more worthy than he is, will take Dante on to Heaven.

Dante agrees, and the two set out.
inferno.2:
It is evening, and Dante is about to follow his guide Virgil down into Hell. But he loses his nerve. Great men have visited the world of the dead before, he says, the hero Aeneas and Saint Paul. He is neither of them.

Virgil tells him that fear is holding him back. He was among the souls in Limbo, the edge of Hell, when a beautiful lady came down from Heaven and called him. She was Beatrice, the woman Dante loved. She begged Virgil to rescue her friend, who was lost and in danger.

Beatrice herself had been sent. A gentle lady in Heaven took pity on Dante and spoke to Saint Lucia, and Lucia went to Beatrice.

With three blessed ladies caring for him, Virgil asks, what is there to fear? Dante's courage returns like a flower opening in the morning sun. He follows Virgil onto the steep, wild road.
inferno.3:
Dante and his guide Virgil come to the gate of Hell. Dark words above it say the gate leads to endless pain, and that all who enter must give up hope. Virgil takes Dante's hand and leads him through.

Inside, the dark air is full of screams. Here are the souls who never took a side in life, neither good nor bad, along with the angels who stayed neutral when others rebelled against God. Neither Heaven nor Hell wants them. They run forever after a whirling banner, stung by wasps and hornets.

Further on, a crowd waits by a river, the Acheron. An old ferryman with eyes of fire, Charon, comes to carry the dead across. He orders Dante away, because Dante is alive, but Virgil tells him this journey is willed in Heaven. Charon falls silent, and the souls drop into his boat like autumn leaves.

Then the ground shakes, a red light flashes, and Dante faints.
inferno.4:
A clap of thunder wakes Dante. He is at the edge of the pit of Hell. His guide Virgil has gone pale, not from fear but from pity, and leads him down into the first circle.

This is Limbo. There are no screams here, only sighs. These souls did no wrong, Virgil explains, but they were never baptized, or they lived before Christ. Their only punishment is to long for God without hope. Virgil is one of them. Only once did a mighty one come and carry souls from here to Heaven, among them Adam, Noah and Moses.

Ahead a light shines in the dark. Four great ancient poets come to greet Virgil, led by Homer, and they welcome Dante into their company. They enter a castle with seven walls. On a meadow inside, Dante sees the heroes and thinkers of the ancient world, among them Caesar, Socrates and Plato. Then Virgil leads him on, back into the dark.
inferno.5:
Dante and his guide Virgil go down to the second circle of Hell. At the entrance stands Minos, a snarling monster who judges the dead. Each soul confesses, and Minos wraps his tail around himself once for every circle it must go down.

Beyond is a dark place where a storm never stops. It throws the souls about like flocks of birds in winter. These are the lustful, people who let desire rule their reason. Virgil points out famous lovers, among them Cleopatra and Helen of Troy.

Dante calls to two souls who fly together. The woman, Francesca, tells their story. One day she and the man beside her were reading alone about the knight Lancelot and his love. When they reached the kiss, he kissed her, and they read no more that day. Love led them both to one death.

As she speaks, her lover weeps. Dante is so filled with pity that he faints.
inferno.6:
Dante wakes in the third circle of Hell. A cold rain of hail, dirty water and snow falls here forever. The gluttons, people who lived to eat and drink, lie in the mud. Over them stands Cerberus, a monstrous dog with three heads, who tears at them. Dante's guide Virgil throws handfuls of earth into the three mouths, and the beast goes quiet.

One soul sits up as they pass. He is Ciacco, a man from Florence, Dante's own city. Dante asks what will become of Florence, which is split into two parties. Ciacco foretells bloodshed. One party will drive out the other, then fall within three years. Pride, envy and greed have set every heart on fire. He asks to be remembered among the living, and sinks back into the mud.

Walking on, Virgil explains that after the last judgment these sinners will feel their pain even more. At the way down waits Plutus, a new enemy.
inferno.7:
At the way down to the fourth circle of Hell, a monster named Plutus shouts strange words at Dante and his guide Virgil. Virgil tells him their journey is willed in Heaven, and Plutus collapses like a sail when the mast breaks.

In the fourth circle two great crowds roll heavy weights with their chests. They crash together, shout at each other, and turn back. One crowd hoarded money. The other wasted it. Many of the hoarders were popes and cardinals.

Dante asks about Fortune. Virgil says she is a servant of God who moves wealth from one people to another. No human wisdom can stop her.

A dark stream leads down to the fifth circle and a marsh called the Styx. In it the angry fight in the mud, striking and biting. Under the water lie the sullen, whose sighs make bubbles on the surface. The two walk around the marsh to the foot of a tower.
inferno.8:
Dante and his guide Virgil stand at the edge of the Styx, the muddy marsh of the fifth circle of Hell, where the angry are punished. A small boat races toward them, steered by the furious boatman Phlegyas, and they step in.

On the way a soul caked with mud rises beside the boat. It is Filippo Argenti, an arrogant man from Florence. Dante curses him, and Virgil praises Dante's anger. Soon the other souls attack Argenti, and Dante is glad.

Ahead rises the city of Dis, the start of lower Hell, its towers glowing red from the fires inside. More than a thousand fallen angels guard the gate. They tell Virgil to stay and send the living man back alone. Virgil goes to talk with them, but they slam the gate in his face.

Virgil returns shaken, yet he tells Dante not to fear. Someone is already coming down who will open the city.
inferno.9:
Dante and his guide Virgil are shut out of Dis, the walled city of lower Hell. Fallen angels have closed the gate. Virgil listens anxiously for help, and his worry frightens Dante. Virgil says he made this journey once before and knows the way.

Suddenly three Furies rise on the burning tower, women stained with blood, with snakes for hair. They scream for Medusa to come and turn Dante to stone. Virgil turns him around and covers his eyes.

Then a sound like a great wind crosses the marsh. A messenger from Heaven walks over the water with dry feet. He opens the gate with a small rod, scolds the fallen angels for resisting God's will, and leaves without a word to the travelers.

They walk in. Inside lies a wide plain of open tombs, with fire burning among them. This is the sixth circle. Here lie the heretics, people who taught false beliefs, with their followers.
inferno.10:
In the sixth circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil walk among burning tombs. Here lie people who believed the soul dies with the body.

A voice calls from one tomb. It is Farinata, a proud nobleman of Florence whose party fought against Dante's family. He stands tall, as if he scorned Hell itself. He boasts that he drove Dante's people out twice. Dante answers that they came back both times, and Farinata's side never did.

A second soul rises beside him, the father of Dante's friend Guido. He asks why his son is not with Dante. Dante speaks of Guido in the past tense, and the father, thinking his son is dead, falls back into the tomb.

Farinata warns that Dante will soon learn how hard it is to return from exile. He explains that the damned see the far future but nothing of the present. Dante asks him to tell the father that Guido is alive.
inferno.11:
In the sixth circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil reach the edge of a cliff. A terrible stench rises from below, so they wait behind a tomb to get used to it. Meanwhile Virgil explains how the rest of Hell is laid out.

Three circles lie below. The first holds the violent, in three rings: those who harmed other people, those who harmed themselves, and those who offended God and nature. The next holds people who cheated strangers, such as flatterers, hypocrites and thieves. The last and smallest holds traitors, who cheated those who trusted them. Fraud is punished lowest because it displeases God most.

Dante asks why the sinners of the upper circles are not down here. Virgil answers that they lacked self control, which offends God less than malice.

Last, Dante asks why lending money at interest is a sin. Virgil says people are meant to live by nature and honest work, and the moneylender scorns both.
inferno.12:
Dante and his guide Virgil climb down a rockslide into the seventh circle of Hell. The Minotaur, the monster of Crete that is half man and half bull, guards the way. Virgil taunts him, and while he thrashes in rage the two slip past.

Below runs a river of boiling blood. In it stand those who did violence to others. Centaurs, creatures half man and half horse, gallop along the bank and shoot arrows at any soul who rises too far out of the blood. Their leader, Chiron, notices that Dante's feet move the stones, so he must be alive. Virgil asks for a guide, and Chiron sends the centaur Nessus.

Nessus leads them along the bank. Tyrants stand in blood up to their eyebrows, among them Alexander. Other killers stand up to their throats, others to the chest. Where the blood covers only the feet, they cross, and Nessus turns back.
inferno.13:
In the seventh circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil enter a wood with no path. The trees are dark, twisted and thorny. Harpies, birds with human faces, nest in the branches.

Virgil tells Dante to break off a twig. The tree cries out in pain, and blood pours from the break. These trees are the souls of people who killed themselves.

The wounded tree was Pier della Vigna, trusted adviser to the emperor Frederick. Envious courtiers turned the emperor against him, and in his shame he took his own life. He explains that such a soul falls here like a seed and grows into a tree. On Judgment Day their bodies will hang from their branches.

Two naked men crash through the wood, chased by black dogs. One hides in a bush, and the dogs tear him apart. The broken bush weeps. It was a man from Florence who hanged himself in his own house.
inferno.14:
In the seventh circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil leave a dark wood and come to a plain of burning sand. Flakes of fire fall slowly on it like snow without wind. Naked souls lie, sit or walk there, slapping at the flames.

One huge man lies scowling as if the fire did not touch him. He is Capaneus, an ancient king who attacked the city of Thebes and was struck down by a thunderbolt. He still shouts his scorn for the gods. Virgil tells him his own rage is his worst punishment.

Along the edge of the wood, they reach a small red stream with stone banks. It puts out the flames above it. Virgil explains where it comes from. Inside a mountain on the island of Crete stands a great old man made of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay. Tears run from cracks in him and flow down to form the rivers of Hell.
inferno.15:
In the seventh circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil walk on a stone bank beside a stream. It crosses a plain of burning sand where fire rains down, and its mist shields them.

A group of souls comes along, squinting up at them. One grabs the hem of Dante's robe. Under the burned face Dante knows Brunetto Latini, a writer from Florence who was his teacher. Brunetto cannot stop, for any soul who stands still here must lie a hundred years under the fire. So he walks beside Dante, who keeps his head bowed in respect.

Brunetto foretells that Dante will win great honor, but that the ungrateful people of Florence will turn against him. Dante thanks him with love for his teaching. He is ready, he says, for whatever fortune brings.

Then Brunetto asks Dante to remember his book, the Treasure, and runs off like the winner of a race.
inferno.16:
In the seventh circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil walk on a stone bank across a plain of burning sand where fire rains down.

Three souls run up, covered in burns. They know Dante by his clothes as a man from Florence, their own city, where they were once famous. They turn in a wheel while they talk. One, Jacopo Rusticucci, names the others, Guido Guerra and Tegghiaio Aldobrandi. Dante has always honored their names and would embrace them if not for the fire.

They ask whether courage and courtesy still live in Florence. Dante cries out that new people and quick money have filled the city with pride. The three ask to be remembered among the living, and run off.

The travelers reach the place where the stream thunders down a cliff. Virgil takes the cord from Dante's waist and throws it into the pit as a signal. Then Dante sees a strange shape swim up through the dark.
inferno.17:
At the edge of the seventh circle of Hell, a monster rises from the pit. It is Geryon, the image of fraud. It has the face of an honest man, the body of a snake, and a scorpion's sting in its tail. It rests its chest on the stone edge beside Dante and his guide Virgil.

While Virgil bargains with the beast, Dante goes alone to see the last sinners here. These are the moneylenders. They sit on the burning sand, brushing at the falling fire like dogs at fleas. Each has a purse hung from his neck, marked with a family emblem, and stares at it.

Dante returns to find Virgil on Geryon's back. Shaking with fear, he climbs on in front, and Virgil holds him. The monster backs off the ledge and swims down through the dark in slow wide circles. He sets them down at the bottom of the cliff and shoots away like an arrow.
inferno.18:
Dante and his guide Virgil have reached the eighth circle of Hell. It is called the Malebolge, which means the evil pouches. It is a field of stone the color of iron, with ten deep ditches one inside another, like the moats around a castle. Stone bridges cross them.

In the first ditch, naked sinners walk in two lines while horned demons whip them from behind. One tries to hide his face, but Dante knows him. He is Venedico Caccianemico, a man from Bologna who talked a young woman into giving herself to a nobleman. From the bridge Virgil points out Jason, the Greek hero who won the Golden Fleece. He is here because he won women with sweet words and then left them.

The second ditch stinks. The people in it are sunk in human filth. These are the flatterers. Dante recognizes Alessio Interminei, a man from Lucca, who admits that his flattering tongue brought him here.
inferno.19:
In the eighth circle of Hell, where fraud is punished, Dante and his guide Virgil look down into the third ditch. Here are churchmen who sold holy things for money.

The rock is full of round holes. Each sinner is stuck in a hole head first, with only his legs showing, and flames burn on the soles of his feet. One pair of legs kicks harder than the rest, so Virgil carries Dante down to it.

The sinner is Pope Nicholas the Third. He cannot see, and he thinks Dante is Boniface, a later pope, come early to take his place. Nicholas admits he used his office to make his family rich. When Boniface arrives, Nicholas will be pushed deeper into the rock, and a worse pope will follow them both.

Dante answers him angrily. Jesus asked Saint Peter for no gold, only to follow him. Greedy popes, he says, have made gold their god. Virgil, pleased, carries Dante back up.
inferno.20:
In the eighth circle of Hell, Dante looks into the fourth ditch. A silent crowd walks slowly along it, weeping. These are fortune tellers and magicians, people who claimed to see the future. Now their heads are twisted around to face backward. Because they tried to look too far ahead, they can only look behind them, and they must walk backward.

Dante weeps to see human bodies so twisted. His guide Virgil scolds him. It is foolish, he says, to pity those whom God has judged.

Virgil names some of the sinners, among them famous seers of ancient Greece. One is Manto, a sorceress who wandered the world and settled on empty land in the middle of a marsh in northern Italy. After she died, people built a city over her bones and called it Mantua. That is the city where Virgil was born, and he wants Dante to know its true beginning.

The moon is setting, and they walk on.
inferno.21:
In the eighth circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil come to the fifth ditch. It is filled with boiling tar. Under the tar are officials who took bribes.

A black demon runs up with a sinner over his shoulder, a town official from Lucca, and throws him in. When the man comes up, other demons under the bridge jab him with hooks until he sinks again.

Virgil tells Dante to hide behind a rock and goes to face the demons alone. They rush at him, but he tells their chief, Malacoda, that Heaven wills this journey. Malacoda drops his hook. He says the next bridge is broken, but there is another one farther on, and he sends ten demons to walk with them.

Dante is terrified of this escort and begs to go without it. Virgil tells him not to worry. The squad marches off, and its leader gives the signal by breaking wind like a trumpet.
inferno.22:
In the eighth circle of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil walk beside a ditch of boiling tar with ten demons as their escort. Under the tar are sinners who took bribes. Some surface for a moment of relief, then dive when the demons come near.

One is too slow. A demon hooks him by the hair and hauls him out like an otter. He says he came from the kingdom of Navarre and took bribes while serving a king. The demons tear at him while he names others in the tar, among them a friar from Sardinia who let his master's enemies go free for money.

Then the sinner plays a trick. If the demons step back, he says, he will whistle and bring up more souls. They step back, and he leaps into the tar and escapes. One demon flies after him and misses. Another attacks the first, and both fall into the tar. Dante and Virgil leave them there.
inferno.23:
Dante and his guide Virgil walk away from the demons who guard the ditch of boiling tar in the eighth circle of Hell. Dante fears the demons will chase them, and they do. Virgil snatches him up and slides down the bank into the next ditch. The demons may not leave their post.

Here the hypocrites walk very slowly, weeping. They wear hooded cloaks that shine with gold on the outside but are made of heavy lead. Two of them are Catalano and Loderingo, friars from Bologna who were once chosen to keep the peace in Florence.

On the ground a man lies nailed down with three stakes, and everyone walks over him. He is Caiaphas, the high priest who said one man should suffer for the people.

Virgil asks the way out. A friar says the bridge here is broken, but they can climb the fallen rocks. So the demon chief lied to them, and Virgil strides off angry.
inferno.24:
Dante and his guide Virgil are deep in the eighth circle of Hell. To leave the ditch of the hypocrites they must climb a slope of broken rock. Virgil pushes Dante up from one boulder to the next. At the top Dante drops down, out of breath. Virgil tells him to get up. No one wins fame lying in bed, he says, and a longer climb is still ahead. Dante goes on.

The next ditch is full of snakes. Thieves run naked among them, with snakes tying their hands behind their backs. A snake bites one man on the neck. He bursts into flame and falls into ashes. Then the ashes gather, and he is himself again, dazed.

He is Vanni Fucci, a violent man from Pistoia who robbed a church treasury and let another take the blame. He is ashamed that Dante has seen him here. To hurt Dante in return, he foretells war and defeat in Tuscany, Dante's homeland.
inferno.25:
In the eighth circle of Hell, among the thieves and the snakes, a thief named Vanni Fucci makes a rude sign at God with both hands. At once snakes wrap around his neck and arms, and he runs off. A centaur, half man and half horse, gallops after him with a fiery dragon on his shoulders. Virgil, Dante's guide, says this is Cacus, a cattle thief killed by Hercules.

Then three more thieves come by. A snake with six legs leaps on one of them, named Agnello, and clings to him. The two melt together like hot wax, until there is one monster that is neither man nor snake.

A small black snake bites a second thief in the belly. Smoke pours from the wound and from the snake's mouth. Slowly they trade shapes. The man becomes a snake and crawls away hissing. The snake stands up as a man. Only the third thief, Puccio, stays as he was.
inferno.26:
Dante begins with bitter words for his own city, Florence. He has just met several of its citizens among the thieves in Hell.

He and his guide Virgil climb to the bridge over the eighth ditch of the eighth circle. Below, the dark is full of small flames, like fireflies in a valley. Each flame hides a sinner.

One flame has two tips. Inside burn Ulysses and Diomedes, the Greek heroes who tricked the city of Troy with the wooden horse. Virgil asks Ulysses how he died.

The flame speaks. Not even love for his son, his father, or his wife could keep him home, Ulysses says. He wanted to know the world. With one ship and a few old friends he sailed out past the limits set for men, into the open ocean. After five months they saw a huge dark mountain. Then a storm rose from it and spun the ship around, and the sea closed over them.
inferno.27:
In the eighth circle of Hell, where sinners burn hidden inside flames, another flame comes up to Dante and his guide Virgil. It asks for news of Romagna, a region of Italy. Dante says there is no open war, though its rulers always want one.

The soul in the flame is Guido da Montefeltro. He believes no one returns from Hell, so he tells his story freely. He was a soldier, famous for cunning. In old age he repented and became a friar.

Then Pope Boniface the Eighth, who was at war with other Christians, asked him how to destroy an enemy town. The pope promised to forgive the sin ahead of time. So Guido gave his advice: promise much and keep little.

When Guido died, Saint Francis came for his soul. But a devil claimed it. A man cannot be forgiven unless he is sorry, the devil argued, and he cannot be sorry for a sin while choosing to commit it.
inferno.28:
In the eighth circle of Hell, Dante looks into the ninth ditch and sees more blood and wounds than he can describe. Here are people who set others against each other and split apart what was joined. A devil with a sword cuts them open as they pass. Their wounds heal as they circle the ditch, and he cuts them again.

Dante sees Mohammed, the prophet of Islam, placed here as a divider of religion, split open from the chin down. Dante's guide Virgil explains that Dante is alive, and the souls stop and stare.

One has lost his tongue, for urging Julius Caesar on to civil war. Mosca, whose words started a feud in Florence, lifts two bleeding stumps.

Last comes a body with no head, carrying its head by the hair like a lantern. He is Bertran de Born, who turned a young king against his father. He parted father and son, so his head is parted from his body.
inferno.29:
In the eighth circle of Hell, Dante keeps staring at the wounded souls in the ninth ditch. His guide Virgil tells him to hurry. Dante explains that he was looking for a relative, Geri del Bello, who was murdered and whose death no one in the family has avenged. Virgil saw him pointing angrily at Dante before he walked away.

They come to the tenth and last ditch. The cries are so pitiful that Dante covers his ears. Here are people who made false things, and they lie in heaps, sick and too weak to stand.

Two sit leaning on each other, covered in scabs, scratching without rest. Both were alchemists who faked precious metals. The first, a man from Arezzo, was burned alive because he joked that he could fly and a foolish man of Siena believed him. Dante remarks how vain the people of Siena are. The second, Capocchio, gladly agrees and mocks the big spenders of that city.
inferno.30:
In the last ditch of the eighth circle of Hell, where people who made false things are punished, two souls run wild, biting the others. One is Gianni Schicchi, who pretended to be a dead man in order to forge his will. The other is Myrrha, who disguised herself to sleep with her own father.

Dante sees a man so swollen with disease that he cannot move. He is Master Adam, who made false gold coins. He is always thirsty and dreams of cool streams.

Beside him lie two liars burning with fever. One of them, Sinon, the Greek who lied to the Trojans about the wooden horse, punches Adam in the belly. Adam hits him in the face. Then they trade insults.

Dante listens, fascinated, until his guide Virgil speaks to him sharply. Dante is too ashamed to answer. Virgil forgives him, but warns him that wanting to hear such a quarrel is a low thing.
inferno.31:
Dante and his guide Virgil leave the last ditch of the eighth circle of Hell. A horn sounds, louder than thunder. Ahead, Dante thinks he sees the towers of a city. Virgil takes his hand and tells him the truth. They are giants, standing around the great pit at the center of Hell, with the rim hiding them from the waist down.

The first giant shouts words that mean nothing. He is Nimrod, whose wicked plan left the world without one shared language, and now no one can understand him. The second, Ephialtes, fought against the gods. He is wrapped in chains, and when he shakes himself Dante is sick with fear.

The third, Antaeus, is not chained. Virgil praises his strength and says that Dante, who is alive, can bring him fame on earth. Antaeus picks them both up. He bends like a leaning tower, sets them down gently at the bottom of Hell, and straightens up again.
inferno.32:
Dante and his guide Virgil stand at the very bottom of Hell, the ninth circle. It is a frozen lake called Cocytus, with ice like glass. Traitors are stuck in it up to their necks, their teeth chattering and their tears freezing in their eyes.

First come those who betrayed their own families. Two brothers are frozen chest to chest, and in their rage they butt heads like goats. Another soul names them.

Farther in are those who betrayed their country. Walking among the heads, Dante kicks one in the face. The soul curses him and will not say who he is. Dante grabs his hair and tears out handfuls, but still he refuses. Then a neighbor calls him Bocca, and Dante knows him as a traitor. Out of spite, Bocca names the other traitors around him.

Then Dante sees two souls frozen in one hole. The one on top is gnawing the other's head. Dante asks him why.
inferno.33:
On the frozen lake at the bottom of Hell, where traitors are locked in ice, a sinner lifts his mouth from the head he is gnawing. He is Count Ugolino of Pisa. The other is Archbishop Ruggieri, who betrayed him.

Ugolino tells Dante how he died. The archbishop locked him in a tower with his four sons. One morning they heard the door nailed shut, and no more food came. The boys offered their father their own flesh to eat. One by one they died in front of him. Blind with hunger, he crawled over their bodies, calling their names. Then hunger did what grief could not. He turns back to the skull.

Farther on, sinners lie on their backs with tears frozen over their eyes. One is Friar Alberigo. He explains that after a betrayal like his, the soul falls here at once, while a demon lives on in the body above. Dante promised to clear his eyes, but leaves without doing it.
inferno.34:
Dante and his guide Virgil reach the very center of Hell. Here those who betrayed their lords lie wholly covered by ice, like straws in glass.

In the middle stands Lucifer, the angel who rebelled against God. He is huge, and frozen in the lake up to his chest. He has three faces and six great wings like a bat's. Their wind freezes the lake. He weeps, and in each mouth he chews a sinner: Judas, who betrayed Jesus, and Brutus and Cassius, who betrayed Julius Caesar.

Then it is time to leave. Dante holds on to Virgil's neck, and Virgil climbs down Lucifer's shaggy side. At the hip he turns upside down and begins to climb up. Dante is confused. Virgil explains that they have passed the center of the earth, and now Lucifer's legs stick up above them.

They follow a small stream up through a dark passage. At last they come out and see the stars again.

purgatorio.1:
Dante and Virgil have climbed out of Hell. It is just before sunrise on Easter morning, and they are standing on the shore of an island on the far side of the world. After so much darkness, Dante is glad simply to see the sky. It is a deep, clear blue, and in it shine four bright stars that only the first man and woman ever saw.

An old man with a long white beard comes up to them. He is Cato, an ancient Roman who chose to die rather than live without freedom, and he guards this shore. He asks how they escaped from Hell. Virgil explains that a lady from Heaven sent him to guide Dante, who is still alive.

Cato lets them pass, but first Dante must be made clean. Down by the water, Virgil washes the soot of Hell from Dante's face with dew. Then he picks a reed and ties it around Dante's waist. At once a new reed grows where the old one was.
purgatorio.2:
It is sunrise on the shore at the foot of Mount Purgatory. Dante and his guide Virgil are still standing by the sea, unsure which way to go.

A light comes racing across the water, faster than any bird. Virgil tells Dante to kneel. It is an angel, driving a boat with nothing but his wings. More than a hundred souls sit in it, singing a psalm together. The angel blesses them, they hurry ashore, and he speeds away.

The new souls notice that Dante is breathing, and they crowd around him in wonder. One of them is Casella, a singer and an old friend. Dante tries three times to hug him, and his arms close on empty air. He asks Casella to sing, and everyone stands still to listen.

Then Cato, the stern old guardian of the shore, shouts at them for wasting time. The souls scatter toward the mountain like startled doves.
purgatorio.3:
Dante and his guide Virgil hurry toward the foot of Mount Purgatory. The sun is behind them, and Dante sees only one shadow on the ground, his own. For a moment he fears Virgil has left him. Virgil reminds him that he is a spirit, and that his body lies buried in Naples. Human reason cannot understand everything, he says. Then he falls silent and sad.

The cliff ahead is too steep to climb. A crowd of souls comes slowly toward them, timid as sheep. They stop in alarm at Dante's shadow.

One of them, fair-haired and handsome, shows Dante his wounds. He is Manfred, a king who died in battle after the Church had cast him out. As he lay dying he turned to God in tears, and God forgave him. Souls like him must wait a long time outside Purgatory, but prayers from the living shorten the wait. He asks Dante to tell his daughter.
purgatorio.4:
On the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory, Dante follows his guide Virgil through a narrow gap in the rock. The path is so steep that he has to use his hands and feet. Worn out, he sits down on a ledge.

Dante is puzzled to see the sun on his left. Virgil explains that they are now on the far side of the world, so the sun crosses the sky the other way. He adds that this mountain is hardest at the bottom. The higher a person climbs, the easier it gets.

A voice nearby says that Dante may need to sit down before then. Behind a boulder, a soul sits hugging his knees. Dante smiles, because it is his lazy friend Belacqua. Belacqua put off turning to God until the end of his life. Now he must wait outside the gate for as many years as he lived, unless someone's prayers help him.
purgatorio.5:
Dante is climbing the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory when the souls behind him point at his shadow. His guide Virgil tells him to keep walking and let people talk.

A new crowd comes along the slope, singing a prayer for mercy. When they see that Dante is alive, they rush toward him. All of them died by violence and were sinners until their last hour. Then they turned to God. They beg Dante to carry news of them home.

Jacopo del Cassero was murdered by an enemy's men and bled to death in a marsh. Buonconte da Montefeltro, a soldier, fled a battle with his throat cut and died saying Mary's name. An angel took his soul. A devil, furious at losing him for a single tear, raised a storm, and the flood swept his body away.

Last comes a woman named Pia. She says only that her husband knows how she died, and asks Dante to remember her.
purgatorio.6:
On the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory, the souls who died by violence press around Dante. Each one begs him to ask the living to pray for them.

Then he asks his guide Virgil a question. Virgil once wrote that prayer cannot change what Heaven has decided. Are these souls hoping for nothing? Virgil says their hope is sound. He was writing about people cut off from God. Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, will explain it better at the top of the mountain.

They see a soul sitting alone, proud and silent as a resting lion. Virgil asks him the way and mentions that he is from Mantua. The soul leaps up. He is Sordello, a poet from the same city, and the two embrace.

At the sight, Dante cries out in anger at Italy, where neighbors make war on each other and no emperor keeps order. He is most bitter about his own city, Florence.
purgatorio.7:
On the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory, the poet Sordello has just embraced a stranger from his home city. Now he asks who the stranger is. It is Virgil, the great poet and Dante's guide. Sordello bows low in amazement. Virgil explains that he comes from Limbo, the sad but painless edge of Hell. He did no wrong, but he lived without the Christian faith.

Sordello warns them that the sun is setting, and no one can climb this mountain in the dark. He leads them to a small valley in the hillside. It is full of grass and flowers brighter than gold or emerald. Souls sit there singing a hymn to Mary.

From the edge, Sordello points them out. They are kings and princes who neglected what they should have done. Among them are the emperor Rudolf, who could have healed Italy and did not, and Henry of England, sitting alone. Sordello remarks that sons are seldom as good as their fathers.
purgatorio.8:
It is evening in a flowery valley on the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory, where kings and princes wait. Dante is there with his guide Virgil and the poet Sordello. One soul leads the others in an evening hymn. Then they all look up in silence.

Two angels fly down, dressed in green, with flaming swords that have no points. Sordello says they have come to guard the valley from a serpent.

Down among the souls, Dante finds a friend, Nino, who was a judge. Nino is astonished that Dante is alive, and asks him to tell his young daughter to pray for him. Then the serpent comes sliding through the grass and flowers. The angels swoop like falcons, and it flees.

Another soul, the nobleman Currado Malaspina, asks for news of his home. Dante praises his family, famous for its generosity and courage. Currado tells him that within seven years he will learn their kindness for himself.
purgatorio.9:
Night has fallen in a valley on the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory, and Dante falls asleep on the grass. Near dawn he dreams that a golden eagle carries him up into fire.

He wakes frightened, because he is somewhere new. His guide Virgil calms him. While Dante slept, Lucia, a lady from Heaven, carried him up to the gate of Purgatory itself.

Three steps lead up to it. The first is white marble, polished like a mirror. The second is dark and cracked. The third is red as blood. An angel sits at the top with a bare sword.

Dante kneels and begs to be let in. With his sword the angel cuts the letter P seven times on Dante's forehead, and tells him to wash these wounds away inside. He unlocks the gate with a silver key and a gold one, and warns that anyone who looks back must go out again. The gate opens with a roar.
purgatorio.10:
Dante and his guide Virgil pass through the gate of Purgatory. They squeeze up a narrow, twisting crack in the rock and come out, tired, on an empty ledge that runs around the mountain. This is the first terrace, where pride is cleansed.

The wall beside them is white marble, carved with scenes so lifelike that they seem to speak. Each shows someone being humble. In one, an angel greets Mary and she accepts God's will. In another, King David dances before the holy ark while his wife looks on with scorn. In the third, the Roman emperor Trajan halts his army to give justice to a poor widow whose son was killed.

Then Virgil points to shapes creeping toward them. At first Dante cannot tell they are people. They are the souls of the proud, bent double under huge stones. Some carry more and some less, and even the most patient seems to weep that he can bear no more.
purgatorio.11:
On the first terrace of Mount Purgatory, the souls of the proud creep along under heavy stones. As they go they say the Lord's Prayer.

Dante's guide Virgil asks them the way to the stairs. A voice from under a stone tells them to come along to the right. The speaker is Umberto, a nobleman from Tuscany. He was so proud of his ancient family that he despised everyone else, and it got him killed.

Another soul knows Dante. It is Oderisi, an artist famous for decorating books. Now he admits that a rival paints better than he did. Fame, he says, is a breath of wind. One painter or poet is praised today, and tomorrow another takes his place.

He points to a soul ahead, Provenzan Salvani, once the lord of Siena and now hardly spoken of. He was allowed up here so soon because he once humbled himself and begged in the public square to free a friend from prison.
purgatorio.12:
On the first terrace of Mount Purgatory, where the proud carry heavy stones, Dante has been walking bent over beside one of them. His guide Virgil tells him to move on.

Virgil tells him to look down. The path is carved with pictures, like the stones over graves, and each shows pride brought low. Dante sees the brightest angel falling from Heaven like lightning. He sees Niobe grieving among her dead children. He sees the weaver Arachne, half turned into a spider, and the city of Troy in ashes.

An angel in white comes to meet them, his face like the morning star. He leads them to a stairway and brushes Dante's forehead with his wings. Voices sing a blessing on the humble.

The climb feels strangely easy, and Dante asks why. Virgil says that one of the seven letters on his forehead is gone. Dante feels with his fingers and finds only six. Virgil smiles.
purgatorio.13:
Dante and his guide Virgil reach the second terrace of Mount Purgatory. It is bare and empty, and the rock is the color of a bruise.

Voices fly past them through the air, though no one can be seen. They call out examples of kindness and love. Virgil explains that this is where envy is cleansed.

Then Dante sees the souls. They sit against the cliff in rough cloaks, leaning on each other like blind beggars at a church door. Their eyelids are sewn shut with iron wire, and tears squeeze through the stitches.

He asks whether anyone is from Italy. A woman named Sapia, from Siena, answers. She says she was happier at other people's bad luck than at her own good luck. When her own townsmen lost a battle, she watched them run and was filled with joy. She made peace with God only at the end of her life. She asks Dante to pray for her.
purgatorio.14:
On the second terrace of Mount Purgatory, where envy is cleansed, the souls sit with their eyes sewn shut. Two of them hear Dante pass and ask who he is. He says only that he comes from a river valley in Tuscany.

One of them is Guido del Duca, a nobleman from the region of Romagna. He guesses that the river is the Arno and says its name deserves to die. The people along it, he says, have turned into beasts. Its waters run past pigs, then snarling dogs, then wolves, then foxes.

Guido admits that envy burned in him whenever he saw someone happy. He mourns the good families of Romagna, now gone or grown wicked. Then he weeps and sends Dante on.

As Dante and his guide Virgil walk away, voices crash past like thunder. They are warnings against envy. Virgil says that Heaven shows people its beauty, and still they stare at the ground.
purgatorio.15:
It is late afternoon on Mount Purgatory. Dante and his guide Virgil are leaving the terrace of envy when a dazzling light strikes Dante's eyes. It is an angel, who sends them up a gentle stairway.

As they climb, Virgil explains why people envy. With earthly goods, the more people share, the less each one gets. Heavenly love is different. The more souls share it, the more each one has.

On the third terrace, Dante is caught up in visions of gentleness. He sees Mary find her lost son in the temple and speak to him softly. He sees a ruler of Athens calmly refuse his wife's call for revenge on a young man who embraced their daughter. He sees a young man being stoned to death, praying for his killers.

Dante comes to himself. Virgil tells him the visions were meant to open his heart to peace. Then a cloud of smoke, black as night, rolls over them.
purgatorio.16:
On the third terrace of Mount Purgatory, where anger is cleansed, the smoke is so thick that Dante cannot open his eyes. He holds the shoulder of his guide Virgil. All around, voices sing a prayer for peace and mercy.

One soul speaks to him. He is Marco, a man from Lombardy. Dante asks him why the world has become so wicked. Some people blame the stars, and some blame human beings.

The stars may nudge people, Marco says, but everyone has free will and the light to tell good from evil. So the fault lies in people themselves.

The soul is born simple, like a child, and needs laws and good leaders to guide it. Rome once had two lights, an emperor for this world and a pope for the road to God. Now the pope has seized both powers, and the Church has fallen in the mud. Light begins to show through the smoke, and Marco turns back.
purgatorio.17:
Dante and his guide Virgil come out of the smoke on the terrace of anger as the sun is setting. Dante's mind fills with visions of what rage destroys. In the last, a girl weeps for her mother, a queen who killed herself in a fury.

A bright light breaks the vision. An angel shows them the stairs, and Dante feels a wing brush his face. As they reach the fourth terrace, night falls and the strength leaves Dante's legs.

While they wait, Virgil explains how the mountain is arranged. Everything people do, good or bad, comes from love. Love can go wrong in three ways. It can aim at harm to others, which gives pride, envy and anger. Those are cleansed on the three terraces below.

It can be too slow in seeking the true good. That is cleansed here, on the fourth. Or it can chase lesser goods too eagerly. That is wept for on the three terraces above.
purgatorio.18:
It is night on the fourth terrace of Mount Purgatory, where souls who were too slow to do good are cleansed. Dante asks his guide Virgil to explain what love is.

Virgil says the soul is made to love. When something pleases it, the soul leans toward that thing and cannot rest until it has it. But not every love is good. Dante is troubled. If love simply comes over people from outside, how can anyone be praised or blamed for it? Virgil answers that people also have reason, which can judge each desire and say yes or no. That power is free will, and it is why people answer for what they choose.

Near midnight a great crowd of souls comes running past. They shout examples of eager haste. One of them, once an abbot in Verona, points the way up without stopping. When they are gone, Dante's thoughts drift, and he falls asleep.
purgatorio.19:
Just before dawn on Mount Purgatory, Dante has a dream. An ugly, stammering woman appears, but as he stares she turns beautiful and begins to sing. She is a Siren, who lures sailors off their course. Then a holy lady calls out, and Virgil, Dante's guide, tears open the Siren's dress. The stench from her belly wakes Dante.

In full daylight an angel sends them up to the fifth terrace. There souls lie face down, weeping, bound hand and foot. These are people who loved money too much. In life they never lifted their eyes from earthly things, so now they are pressed to the earth.

Dante speaks with one of them, Pope Adrian the Fifth. He was pope for little more than a month, and only then saw how empty his greed had been. Dante kneels, but Adrian tells him to stand, since here they are equals. Then he asks to be left to his weeping.
purgatorio.20:
On the fifth terrace of Mount Purgatory, the greedy lie face down, weeping. Dante and his guide Virgil pick their way along the cliff wall. Dante curses greed as a wolf whose hunger is never filled.

He hears one soul calling out examples of people who chose poverty or gave freely. The soul is Hugh Capet, founder of the family of kings who rule France. He says his family did little harm at first, but turned to lies, robbery and murder once it grew rich. He foresees worse. One French prince will ruin Florence by treachery, another will sell his own daughter, and a French king will seize the pope himself.

Hugh explains that by day the souls recall generous people, and by night they recall famous misers and thieves.

As the two poets walk on, the whole mountain shakes, and every soul cries out glory to God. Dante is frightened and burns to know why, but he dares not ask.
purgatorio.21:
Dante and his guide Virgil are walking on the fifth terrace of Mount Purgatory, where the greedy lie face down. The mountain has just shaken, and Dante longs to know why.

A spirit comes up behind them. Virgil explains that Dante is still alive, and asks about the earthquake. The spirit says the mountain shakes only when a soul feels itself clean and free to rise, and then all the others shout for joy. He is that soul. After more than five hundred years lying here, he has just been set free.

He is Statius, a Roman poet. He says he owes all his poetry to Virgil's great poem, the Aeneid, and would gladly spend another year in Purgatory to have lived when Virgil did. Dante cannot help smiling. He tells Statius who is standing in front of him. Statius bends to embrace Virgil's feet, but Virgil stops him gently, since both are only shades.
purgatorio.22:
An angel has wiped another mark of sin from Dante's forehead, and he climbs toward the sixth terrace of Mount Purgatory feeling lighter. With him are two poets, his guide Virgil and Statius, a soul who has just finished his cleansing.

Virgil asks how so wise a man could have been greedy. Statius laughs. His fault was the opposite one. He threw money away, and wasteful spending is punished on the same terrace as greed. Virgil then asks how he became a Christian. Statius says Virgil himself showed the way. Lines Virgil wrote about a new age matched what the first Christians were preaching. Statius was baptized, but out of fear he kept his faith secret.

On the sixth terrace they find a tree, narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, heavy with sweet fruit and sprinkled by falling water. A voice in its leaves forbids the fruit and praises people who ate and drank little.
purgatorio.23:
On the sixth terrace of Mount Purgatory, Dante walks with two poets, his guide Virgil and Statius. They hear singing mixed with weeping. A crowd of souls overtakes them, so thin that their skin clings to their bones.

One of them stares at Dante. Dante knows him only by his voice. It is Forese, an old friend who died a few years ago. Forese explains that these souls ate and drank too much in life. Now the smell of fruit on a tree and of water falling on its leaves fills them with hunger and thirst, and that longing makes them clean.

Dante wonders how Forese has climbed so high so soon. Forese says the prayers and tears of his widow Nella carried him up. He warns that the shameless women of Florence will soon be punished.

Then Dante tells him how Virgil has led him, still alive, through Hell and up the mountain, toward Beatrice, the woman Dante loved.
purgatorio.24:
On the sixth terrace of Mount Purgatory, where souls who ate and drank too much grow thin with hunger, Dante walks beside his old friend Forese. Forese points out the souls nearby, among them a pope who loved eels and wine.

One of them, Buonagiunta, a poet from Lucca, asks whether Dante wrote a famous new kind of love poem. Dante answers that he writes down what Love speaks inside him. Buonagiunta says he now sees what held older poets like himself back.

Forese asks when they will meet again. Dante does not know, but says Florence grows worse every day. Forese foresees that the man most to blame will be dragged to Hell at a beast's tail.

Dante and his guides, Virgil and Statius, pass a second fruit tree, where a voice recalls gluttons. Then a glowing red angel shows them the way up, and Dante feels the wind of its wing on his forehead.
purgatorio.25:
Dante climbs a narrow stair toward the seventh terrace of Mount Purgatory with two poets, his guide Virgil and Statius. He is puzzled. On the terrace below he saw souls wasted by hunger. How can a spirit that needs no food grow thin?

Virgil asks Statius to answer. Statius explains how a child is formed in the womb. The father's blood shapes the growing body. When the brain is complete, God breathes in a new spirit, which gathers everything into a single soul. At death that soul leaves the flesh and keeps its powers. It shapes the air around it into a body, as sunlight makes a rainbow in wet air. This body of air is called a shade. It can see, speak and weep, and it shows whatever the soul feels.

They reach the last terrace. Flames shoot out from the cliff, leaving only a narrow path. Inside the fire, souls walk singing and calling out examples of pure and faithful love.
purgatorio.26:
On the last terrace of Mount Purgatory, souls guilty of lust walk through fire. Dante follows his guide Virgil along the narrow edge. His body casts a shadow on the flames, and the souls ask how he can still be alive.

Before he answers, a second crowd arrives from the other direction. The two groups kiss in greeting, then part. Each shouts an example of its own sin. One group loved their own sex. The other loved the opposite sex, but followed their desires like animals.

Dante explains that a lady in Heaven has won him this journey. The soul who questioned him is Guido Guinicelli, a poet Dante honors as the father of sweet love poetry in Italian. Guido points to a better craftsman ahead, then sinks into the fire like a fish into water. The other is Arnaut, a famous poet of love songs. He asks Dante to remember his pain, and hides himself in the flames.
purgatorio.27:
At sunset on the last terrace of Mount Purgatory, an angel stands beyond a wall of fire. He says that no one goes farther without passing through the flames.

Dante is terrified and will not move. His guide Virgil promises that the fire will hurt but cannot kill him. Still Dante stands frozen. Then Virgil says that only this wall stands between him and Beatrice, the woman he loved. At her name Dante gives way. He walks in behind Virgil. The heat is so fierce that he would jump into molten glass to cool off. A singing voice leads them out.

Night falls, and they sleep on the steps. Dante dreams of a young woman gathering flowers in a meadow.

At dawn they climb to the top of the stair. Virgil says he can see no farther. Dante's will is now free and sound, and he should follow it. Virgil crowns him master of himself.
purgatorio.28:
At the top of Mount Purgatory, Dante walks into a green forest at dawn. A soft breeze stirs the leaves and birds sing in the branches. Behind him come his guide Virgil and the poet Statius.

A stream stops him. On the far bank a beautiful woman walks alone, singing and picking flowers. Dante asks her to come nearer, and she comes smiling to the water's edge.

She explains where they are. This is the garden God gave the first humans, who lost it through their own fault. The mountain rises above all storms, so the breeze here comes only from the turning of the heavens. The water flows from a spring fed by God's will and divides into two rivers. This one, Lethe, washes away the memory of sin. The other, Eunoe, brings back the memory of every good deed.

She adds that the ancient poets who sang of a Golden Age were perhaps dreaming of this place.
purgatorio.29:
In the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory, Dante walks along a stream. On the other bank walks a beautiful woman. She tells him to look and listen.

A great light sweeps through the forest, and sweet music fills the air. Something like seven golden trees comes toward them. Closer, Dante sees they are seven tall candlesticks, whose flames leave bands of color in the air like a rainbow. He turns to Virgil, his guide, and Virgil looks just as amazed.

Behind the lights comes a slow procession. First walk twenty-four elders in white, crowned with lilies. Then come four winged creatures covered with eyes. Between them rolls a chariot pulled by a griffin, a creature half eagle and half lion. Three women dance at its right wheel and four at its left. Seven old men follow, crowned with red flowers.

When the chariot is opposite Dante, thunder sounds, and the whole procession stops.
purgatorio.30:
In the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory, a great procession has stopped in front of Dante. A hundred angels rise on the chariot at its center, singing and throwing flowers.

Through the cloud of flowers a lady appears, veiled in white. Before he sees her face, Dante feels the old love that first struck him as a boy. He turns to tell his guide Virgil. But Virgil is gone, and Dante weeps.

The lady calls him by name and tells him to save his tears, for he will have more to weep about. She is Beatrice, the woman he loved. Dante hangs his head. When the angels sing in pity, he breaks down.

Beatrice tells the angels why she is harsh. Dante had great gifts, and while she lived she kept him on the right road. After she died he chased false pleasures. He fell so low that only a journey among the damned could save him.
purgatorio.31:
In the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory, Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, stands on a chariot across a stream from him. She has accused him of turning away from her after her death, and demands that he confess.

Dante can hardly speak. He forces out a weak yes and bursts into tears. He admits that false pleasures led him astray once her face was hidden. Beatrice says her death should have taught him not to trust in passing things. She orders him to lift his head. Even veiled, she is more beautiful than before. His remorse is so sharp that he faints.

He wakes in the river Lethe, whose water takes away the memory of sin. The lady of the garden pulls him across and dips his head so that he drinks. Four maidens lead him to Beatrice, and he gazes into her eyes. Then three more maidens beg her to show her face, and Beatrice lifts her veil.
purgatorio.32:
In the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory, Dante stares at Beatrice, the woman he loved, until her brightness dazzles him. The holy procession turns, and he follows her chariot through the forest.

They stop at a bare tree, the one Adam ate from. The griffin that pulls the chariot ties its pole to the trunk, and the tree bursts into blossom. Dante falls asleep. When he wakes, Beatrice sits at the root of the tree with seven maidens, guarding the chariot. She tells him to watch, and to write down what he sees.

An eagle swoops down and strikes the chariot. A fox leaps in, and Beatrice drives it out. The eagle returns and leaves its feathers behind. A dragon rises and tears away part of the floor. Then the chariot sprouts seven horned heads. A shameless woman sits on it, kissing a giant. When she glances at Dante, the giant beats her and drags the monster into the forest.
purgatorio.33:
In the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory, seven maidens weep over the holy chariot, which Dante has just seen turned into a monster and dragged away. Beatrice, the woman he loved, listens in sorrow. Then she walks on and calls Dante to her side.

She foretells that God will soon send someone to destroy the shameless woman and the giant who took the chariot. Her words are a riddle, she admits, but events will explain it. Dante must carry what he has seen back to the living.

Dante says he cannot remember ever turning away from her. She smiles. He has drunk from Lethe, the river that washes away the memory of sin.

At noon they reach a spring where two rivers part. Matilda, the lady of the garden, leads Dante and the poet Statius to drink from the second river, Eunoe. Dante comes back made new, clean and ready to rise to the stars.

paradiso.1:
Dante begins by asking the god Apollo for help, because this last part of his story is the hardest to tell. He has been to Heaven, he says, and seen things that no one can fully remember or put into words.

It is noon in the garden at the top of Mount Purgatory. Beatrice, the woman Dante has loved since he was a boy, turns and looks straight into the sun. Dante looks too, then fixes his eyes on her. As he watches her, he feels himself become something more than human. The light grows brighter, and he hears a music he has never heard before.

He does not understand what is happening, so Beatrice tells him. He is no longer on the earth. He is rising faster than lightning. Everything God made, she explains, is drawn toward its proper place. Now that Dante is free of sin, rising toward God is as natural for him as a river running downhill.
paradiso.2:
Dante begins with a warning to his readers. Those in small boats should turn back, because he is sailing into waters no one has crossed before.

Then he and Beatrice, the woman he loved and now his guide through Heaven, rise as fast as an arrow. They arrive at the Moon, the first of the heavens. It takes them in like a shining cloud.

Dante asks what causes the dark patches on the Moon. He thinks some parts are made of thinner stuff than others. Beatrice shows him he is wrong. If the Moon were thin right through, sunlight would pass through it in an eclipse. If it were thin only partway, the light would still bounce back just as bright.

The true cause lies deeper, she says. God's power flows down through the heavens and joins with each star in a different way. That is what makes one part shine brightly and another dimly.
paradiso.3:
In the heaven of the Moon, Dante sees faint faces, as dim as reflections in still water. He takes them for reflections and turns to look behind him. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide through Heaven, smiles at his mistake. These are real souls, she says, placed here because they failed to keep holy vows.

Dante speaks to the most eager one. She is Piccarda, a woman he once knew. He asks whether the souls here wish for a higher place. She says they do not. Love makes them want only what God wants, and in his will is their peace.

Piccarda then tells her story. She became a nun as a girl, but violent men dragged her from the convent. Beside her shines the Empress Constance, who was also forced out but stayed a nun at heart. Then Piccarda sings a hymn to Mary and sinks out of sight, like a weight through deep water.
paradiso.4:
In the heaven of the Moon, Dante is torn between two questions and says nothing. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide through Heaven, reads both in his face.

First, do souls return to live in the stars, as the Greek thinker Plato taught? No, she says. Every blessed soul lives in the highest heaven with God. The souls appeared on the Moon only as a sign, to show that their share of joy is the smallest.

Second, the nuns he just met were dragged from their convents. Why are they blamed? Because a will that truly refuses cannot be bent. Once free, they could have gone back, and they did not. In their hearts they never agreed, but out of fear they gave way.

Dante then asks one thing more. Can a person make up for a broken vow with other good deeds? Beatrice looks at him with eyes so full of love that he has to look down.
paradiso.5:
In the heaven of the Moon, Dante has asked whether a broken vow can be made up for with some other good deed. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide through Heaven, answers.

God's greatest gift to people is free will, she says. In a vow, a person freely gives that gift back to God. Nothing is worth as much, so nothing can replace it. The promise must always be kept. The Church may let someone change the thing promised, but only for something greater. So no one should vow lightly. A foolish vow is better admitted as a mistake than kept.

Then the two shoot upward like an arrow into the second heaven, the planet Mercury. More than a thousand shining souls come toward them, like fish in a pond rising to be fed. One invites Dante to ask anything. Dante asks who he is. The soul glows so brightly with joy that it is hidden in its own light.
paradiso.6:
In the heaven of Mercury, a shining soul answers Dante. He is Justinian, a Roman emperor. After a pope corrected his faith, he says, he gave himself to his great work, putting the laws of Rome in order.

Justinian tells the story of the eagle, the banner of Rome. It came to Italy with the Trojan hero Aeneas. Rome's kings and heroes carried it to victory over every enemy. Julius Caesar bore it across Europe, and under Augustus it brought the whole world peace. Under the next emperor Christ was crucified, which Justinian calls the eagle's greatest glory.

Now, he says, both parties in Italy do wrong. One fights against the eagle, and the other claims it for itself.

Mercury holds souls who did good deeds because they wanted fame, and they are content with their place. Among them is Romeo, a poor pilgrim who served a count faithfully, was falsely accused, and went away to beg his bread in old age.
paradiso.7:
In the heaven of Mercury, the souls sing and speed away. Dante is left with a question he is too shy to ask. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide through Heaven, answers it.

If Christ's death was a just punishment, how could those who killed him be justly punished too? Beatrice explains that Christ was both human and divine. The human nature he took on deserved punishment for the sin of Adam, the first man. But the person who suffered was God, so killing him was a wrong.

Why did God save people this way? Humanity could never humble itself enough to pay for its own sin. God could simply have forgiven. Instead he chose both to forgive and to pay the debt himself, by becoming a man.

Last, she explains why some things decay. What God makes directly, like the angels and the human soul, lasts forever. And since God made the first human bodies directly, bodies will rise again.
paradiso.8:
Dante does not feel himself rising. He knows he has reached the third heaven, the planet Venus, only because Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide, has grown more beautiful. Lights rush toward him, singing.

One of them speaks. He is Charles Martel, a young prince who was Dante's friend and died early. Had he lived, he says, he would have ruled several lands, and much evil would have been avoided. He warns that his brother is greedy and rules badly.

Dante asks how a generous father can have a mean son. Charles explains that people must live together, and a society needs many kinds of people, from lawmakers to soldiers to priests. So the heavens give each person a different nature, without regard to family. Otherwise children would always be just like their parents.

The trouble, he adds, is that the world ignores these gifts. It forces a born soldier into the Church and makes a king of a born preacher.
paradiso.9:
In the heaven of Venus, the young prince Charles Martel tells Dante of wrongs his family will suffer, then turns back toward God.

Another light comes near. She is Cunizza, a noblewoman from northern Italy and sister of a cruel tyrant. She is here, she says, because this star of love ruled her life. She gladly forgives herself for that and feels no grief. She then foretells blood and treachery in the cities of her homeland.

Next speaks Folco, from the city of Marseilles. When he was young he burned with love. But here no one feels regret, he says. The souls smile at the wisdom of God, who planned it all.

Folco points to the light beside him. It is Rahab, the woman in the Bible who helped Joshua win the Holy Land. The Pope, he says bitterly, has forgotten the Holy Land. He and his cardinals think only of money and church law. But Rome will soon be free of them.
paradiso.10:
Dante asks the reader to look up and admire how well God has ordered the heavens. The slanted path of the sun and planets is set at just the right angle to keep the earth alive.

Then, without feeling the climb, he is inside the Sun, the fourth heaven. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide, tells him to thank God. He does so with such love that for a moment he forgets even her.

Lights brighter than the Sun form a ring around the two of them. They circle three times, singing, then pause like dancers waiting for the music. One speaks. He is Thomas Aquinas, a great teacher of the Church. He names the other eleven lights in the ring, all men famous for wisdom. Among them are his own teacher Albert and one whose wisdom, he says, no one has ever matched.

Then the ring turns again and sings, as sweetly as a clock chiming before dawn.
paradiso.11:
Dante thinks how foolish people are to chase money, power, and pleasure, while he stands in Heaven. He is in the Sun, where a ring of wise souls surrounds him and Beatrice, the woman he loved.

Thomas Aquinas, a great teacher and a friar of Saint Dominic's order, speaks from the ring. God sent two leaders to guide the Church, he says. He will tell of one, Saint Francis.

Francis was born in Assisi. As a young man he defied his father and took Poverty as his bride, a lady no one had wanted since Christ died. Others saw their joy and followed him barefoot. On a mountain he received the wounds of Christ in his body. Dying, he left Poverty to his brothers and asked to lie on the bare ground.

Saint Dominic was a leader just as worthy, Thomas says. But most of Dominic's friars now wander after rich pastures like greedy sheep. Only a few stay close to their shepherd.
paradiso.12:
In the heaven of the Sun, Thomas Aquinas falls silent and his ring of wise souls begins to turn. A second ring forms around it, and the two circle and sing like a double rainbow. Then both stop at once.

A voice speaks from the new ring. Thomas, a follower of Saint Dominic, praised Saint Francis. So this speaker, a follower of Francis, will praise Dominic.

Dominic was born in Spain. His mother foresaw the great things he would do. He studied for love of truth, not for money, and became a great teacher. He asked the Pope for only one thing, leave to fight false beliefs. Then he went out like a mountain flood and struck where they were strongest.

The speaker complains that his own Franciscans have left the path of Francis. Some make his rule too loose and others too strict. He is Bonaventure, once head of that order, and he names the other souls in his ring.
paradiso.13:
In the heaven of the Sun, two rings of shining souls wheel around Dante in opposite directions. They sing of God, then stop.

Thomas Aquinas, the great teacher of the Church, speaks again. Earlier he said that one soul in his ring had wisdom no one ever matched. This puzzles Dante. Surely Adam, the first man, and Christ were wiser, since God made them directly.

Thomas agrees about Adam and Christ. What God makes with his own hand is perfect, while nature works like an artist with a shaking hand. But he was speaking only of kings. The soul is Solomon, the king in the Bible. When God offered him anything, he asked for the wisdom to rule well, not for answers to puzzles of philosophy. Among kings, no one has matched him.

Thomas draws a lesson. People should be slow to say yes or no, and slow to judge others. A thorn bush that looks dead all winter may bear a rose.
paradiso.14:
In the heaven of the Sun, Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, asks the wise souls a question for him. When the dead rise and have their bodies again, will the souls still shine like this? And will such light not hurt their eyes?

A gentle voice from the inner ring answers. Their light will last forever, because it comes from their love of God. With their bodies back they will be whole. They will see God better, love more, and shine brighter, and their eyes will be strong enough to bear it. Both rings cry Amen so eagerly that Dante sees how they long for their bodies, and for their mothers and fathers too.

Then Dante finds himself lifted to a redder star, the planet Mars, the fifth heaven. Before him two beams of light form a cross, and on it Christ flashes like lightning. A hymn he cannot follow rings out from the cross, and it holds him more sweetly than anything before.
paradiso.15:
In the heaven of Mars, the souls of those who fought for the faith shine in the shape of a great cross. They fall silent so that Dante may speak. One light shoots down to the foot of the cross like a falling star and greets him as its own blood.

The soul thanks God for such favor to its descendant. Dante glances at Beatrice, the woman he loved, who smiles, and he asks the soul its name.

It is Cacciaguida, his great-great-grandfather. He describes the Florence of his day, a small city inside its old walls, peaceful and modest. Women wore no jewels or face paint. Mothers rocked the cradle themselves and told old stories as they spun. No wife was left alone while her husband went off to France.

Cacciaguida was born and baptized there. Later he followed the Emperor Conrad on a crusade, was made a knight, and died fighting. From that death he came to the peace of Heaven.
paradiso.16:
In the heaven of Mars, Dante feels proud of his noble blood. He admits that such pride is foolish, since nobility is a cloak that time keeps trimming unless something is added each day. He speaks to his ancestor Cacciaguida, a knight who died on crusade, with special respect, and Beatrice, the woman he loved, smiles at it.

Dante asks about his family and about Florence in the old days. Cacciaguida says only that he and his forebears were born inside the old city. Florence then had a fifth of the people it has now, and they were true Florentines.

The trouble came, he says, when families from the countryside moved in. Mixing peoples always makes a city sick. He lists the great houses he knew, many now ruined or forgotten.

Last he names the quarrel that ended the peace. A young man, Buondelmonte, ran from his wedding, and was killed for it. Before that, Cacciaguida says, Florence had no reason to weep.
paradiso.17:
In the heaven of Mars, Dante is with Cacciaguida, his great-great-grandfather. In Hell and in Purgatory, Dante heard dark hints about his future. Now he asks to know it plainly. A blow that is expected, he says, hurts less.

Cacciaguida sees the future in God's mind. Dante will be driven out of Florence through lies, by a plot made at the Pope's court. He will leave everything he loves. He will learn how bitter another man's bread tastes, and how hard it is to climb another man's stairs. His fellow exiles will turn on him, and he will do best to stand alone. A generous lord in northern Italy will shelter him first.

Dante has one more worry. If he writes all he has seen, many will hate him. If he holds back, he fears he will be forgotten. Cacciaguida tells him to tell the whole truth and let the guilty squirm. His words will taste bitter at first, then nourish.
paradiso.18:
In the heaven of Mars, Dante is thinking over what the soul of his ancestor has just told him, some sweet and some bitter. Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide through Heaven, tells him to take heart. Her face is so full of love that he forgets everything else.

His ancestor points to the cross of light where the souls of holy warriors shine. As he names them, each one flashes like lightning: Joshua, Charlemagne, Roland, and others.

Then Dante rises to the next heaven, the white planet Jupiter. Here the souls of just rulers fly like flocks of birds and form letters in the sky. They spell out a Latin sentence telling the rulers of the earth to love justice. The last letter, an M, changes into the head and neck of an eagle.

Dante prays that God will punish the people in the Church who buy and sell holy things and care more for money than for the saints.
paradiso.19:
In the heaven of Jupiter, the souls of just rulers have formed the shape of a great eagle. Then the eagle speaks. Though made of many souls, it speaks with one voice and calls itself I.

Dante has a question that has troubled him for years. Suppose a man is born in far-off India, where no one has ever heard of Christ. He lives a good life and dies without baptism. How can it be just to shut him out of Heaven?

The eagle answers that God's justice is too deep for human minds. A person can see the bottom of the sea near the shore but not far out. Whatever God wills is just, and people on earth are in no position to judge it.

Yet many who call on Christ, it adds, will stand farther from him than some who never knew his name. The eagle ends by listing the Christian kings of Dante's day and their shameful deeds.
paradiso.20:
In the heaven of Jupiter, the eagle made of the souls of just rulers falls silent while the souls sing. Then a murmur like a mountain stream rises through its neck and becomes a voice.

The eagle tells Dante to look at its eye, where its six greatest souls shine. The pupil is David, the king of Israel who wrote the Psalms. Around him are five others, among them the Roman emperors Trajan and Constantine, and Ripheus, a Trojan warrior who lived long before Christ.

Dante is astonished. How can two pagans be in Heaven? The eagle explains that neither died a pagan. Trajan was in Hell, but prayers full of hope brought him back to life, and he believed. Ripheus loved what was right so deeply that God showed him the salvation to come, and he believed.

So people on earth, the eagle warns, should be slow to judge who is saved. Even the souls in Heaven do not know everyone God has chosen.
paradiso.21:
Dante and Beatrice, the woman he loved and his guide, rise to Saturn, the seventh heaven. Beatrice does not smile. Her beauty grows with every heaven, she explains, and here her smile would burn him to ash.

Dante sees a golden ladder climbing so high that he cannot see its top. Countless lights come down its steps, the souls of people who gave their lives to prayer. One stops near him. Dante asks why there is no singing here. The soul answers that his mortal ears could not bear it.

Dante asks why this soul, out of all of them, was chosen to greet him. The soul says not even the highest angel can answer that, and people on earth should stop prying into God's hidden plans.

He is Peter Damian, a monk from a mountain hermitage who later became a cardinal. He rages at the fat, pampered churchmen of Dante's time. The other souls gather round and give a cry like thunder.
paradiso.22:
In the heaven of Saturn, a thunderous cry from the souls has frightened Dante. He turns to Beatrice, the woman he loved, like a child running to its mother. She calms him. The cry, she says, was a prayer for God's justice, which will come in its own time.

The brightest soul comes forward. He is Saint Benedict, who founded the monastery of Monte Cassino and wrote a rule for monks. Dante asks to see his face without the light that hides it. Benedict says that wish will be granted in the highest heaven, where the golden ladder ends.

Then he grieves. No one climbs that ladder now. His rule is wasted paper, and the monasteries have become dens of thieves.

The souls sweep upward, and Dante follows. He arrives among the fixed stars, in the Twins, the sign he was born under. Beatrice tells him to look down. He sees the seven planets below him, and the earth so small that he smiles.
paradiso.23:
Dante is in the eighth heaven, among the fixed stars. Beatrice, the woman he loved, watches the sky like a mother bird waiting for dawn. Soon she cries out that the armies of Christ are coming.

Dante sees thousands of lights, the souls of the saved, and above them one sun that lights them all. It is Christ. The brightness is more than Dante can bear, and his mind seems to burst out of itself. Afterward he is strong enough to look at Beatrice's smile, though he cannot describe it.

Christ rises higher to spare Dante's eyes. Now Dante can see the brightest light that remains, the Virgin Mary. An angel comes down like a ring of fire, circles her as a crown, and sings more sweetly than any music on earth.

Mary rises after her son, and the souls stretch up toward her like children reaching for their mother. They stay, singing a hymn to her, and Saint Peter is among them.
paradiso.24:
In the heaven of the fixed stars, Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, asks the souls of the saints to share their wisdom with him. They answer by whirling in circles. The brightest comes forward. He is Saint Peter, the first leader of the Church, and Beatrice asks him to test Dante on faith.

Dante gets ready like a student before an examination. Peter asks what faith is. Dante says it is the ground of what people hope for and the proof of things they cannot see. Peter asks where his faith came from. From the Bible, Dante answers.

Why trust the Bible? Because of the miracles. How can he be sure the miracles happened? Dante replies that if the whole world became Christian through a few poor men without any miracles, that would be the greatest miracle of all.

Dante then states what he believes: one God in three persons. Peter is so pleased that he sings a blessing and circles Dante three times.
paradiso.25:
Dante begins with a wish. He hopes his poem will soften Florence, the city that has shut him out, so that he can go home and be crowned as a poet in the church where he was baptized.

He is in the heaven of the fixed stars, and a second light joins Saint Peter. It is Saint James, the apostle whose shrine in Spain draws pilgrims. James tests Dante on hope. Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, answers one part for him: no Christian has more hope than he does. Dante then says that hope is the sure expectation of the glory to come. He learned it from the Psalms and from James's own letter.
