A third light arrives. It is Saint John, the apostle who was closest to Jesus. Dante stares to see whether John has his body with him, and the brightness blinds him. John tells him his body is still in the earth. Dante turns to Beatrice and cannot see her.
paradiso.26:
Dante has been blinded by the light of the apostle Saint John, in the heaven of the fixed stars. John tells him his sight will return, because Beatrice, the woman he loved, can heal it. Meanwhile John tests him on love.

Dante says that what he loves above all is God. John asks what led him there. Reason and the Bible both taught him, Dante answers. Good things draw love, and God is the highest good. He is also drawn by the world's existence, his own life, Christ's death, and the hope of Heaven.

All Heaven sings, and Beatrice's eyes clear his sight. He sees better than before and notices a fourth light. It is Adam, the first man.

Adam answers what Dante longs to know. His sin was not eating the fruit itself but going beyond the limit God set. His language died out long ago, since all human speech changes. And he stayed in the garden of Eden only about six hours.
paradiso.27:
In the heaven of the fixed stars, all the saints sing glory to God, and Dante is drunk with joy. Then Saint Peter, the first pope, turns red with anger, and the whole sky reddens with him.

Peter says that the man who holds his place in Rome has turned the Church into a sewer. The early popes gave their blood for the faith, not to gain gold. They never meant their keys to fly on banners in wars against Christians. God will send help soon, and Dante must tell the world what he has heard.

The saints rise out of sight like snow falling upward. Dante looks down at the earth. Then one look from Beatrice, the woman he loved, lifts him to the ninth heaven, the fastest of all. Its turning moves every heaven below it, and time itself begins there.

Beatrice mourns that greed drowns everyone and only children stay innocent. But she promises that a great change is coming.
paradiso.28:
Dante is in the ninth heaven, the swiftest one, with Beatrice, the woman he loved. He sees a light reflected in her eyes and turns to find it. It is a single point, tiny and too bright to look at. Around it spin nine rings of fire. The closest ring is the fastest and brightest, and each one farther out is slower.

Beatrice tells him that all of heaven and nature hang from that point. It is God, and the rings are the angels.

Dante is puzzled. In the universe he knows, the outer heavens are the fastest and most holy. Here it is the inner rings. Beatrice explains that he should measure by power, not by size. The ring that loves and knows God most matches the largest heaven.

The rings blaze and sing. Beatrice names the nine orders of angels, from the Seraphim nearest God down to the Angels. Their joy, she says, comes first from seeing God, and love follows.
paradiso.29:
In the ninth heaven, Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, gazes at the point of light that is God. Then she answers questions about the angels that Dante has not yet asked.

God did not create in order to gain anything, she says. He created so that his light could shine back from other beings. The angels, the heavens, and raw matter all came into being in one instant. Almost at once some angels fell, through the pride of Lucifer, whom Dante saw crushed at the bottom of the world. The rest stayed humble, and they have circled God in joy ever since.

Beatrice then turns on the preachers of earth. They invent their own stories and tell jokes to make crowds laugh, while the Gospel goes unspoken. People go home fed on wind and put their trust in worthless pardons.

She ends with the angels. They are beyond counting, and each one receives God's light in its own way, yet God remains one.
paradiso.30:
The rings of angels fade like stars at dawn, and Dante turns to Beatrice, the woman he loved. Her beauty is so great that he gives up trying to describe it.

She tells him they have left the last turning heaven and entered the Empyrean, the heaven of pure light. A flash blinds him, and then he can see better than ever.

He sees a river of light between banks of flowers. Sparks fly out, settle on the flowers, and dive back in. When he bathes his eyes in the water, the river becomes a circle, and the flowers and sparks turn out to be saints and angels. The saints sit in more than a thousand rows, like the petals of a vast white rose.

Beatrice leads him to its golden center. The seats are nearly full. One empty throne waits for Henry, an emperor who will come to set Italy right. A pope will work against him and be punished in Hell.
paradiso.31:
In the highest heaven, Dante looks at the saints, seated in rows like the petals of a great white rose. Angels fly down among them and up again to God, like bees going between flowers and the hive. Their faces are flame and their wings gold.

Dante is as stunned as a traveler from the wild north seeing Rome. He turns to ask Beatrice, the woman he loved, about what he sees. She is gone. An old man with a kind face stands in her place.

The old man says Beatrice sent him, and points to her seat high in the rose. Dante sees her there, crowned with light. He thanks her for leading him from slavery to freedom. Far away, she smiles at him, then turns back toward God.

The old man is Saint Bernard, a monk devoted to the Virgin Mary. He tells Dante to look up to the top row. There Mary shines among a thousand rejoicing angels.
paradiso.32:
In the highest heaven, the saints sit in rows like the petals of a white rose. Saint Bernard, the monk who is now Dante's guide, explains how they are arranged.

At the top sits the Virgin Mary. Below her is Eve, the first woman, and then a line of women from the Hebrew Bible running down the rose. This line divides the rose in two. On one side are those who believed in Christ before he came, on the other those who believed after. Across from Mary sits John the Baptist, with Saint Francis and other saints beneath him.

The lower rows are filled with children who died before they could choose right or wrong. Dante wonders why some sit higher than others. Bernard says God gives his grace as he pleases.

The angel Gabriel sings to Mary, and all Heaven answers. Bernard points out Adam and Saint Peter beside her. Then he begins a prayer to Mary, asking her to help Dante see God.
paradiso.33:
In the highest heaven, Saint Bernard, the monk guiding Dante, prays to the Virgin Mary. He asks her to clear Dante's eyes so that he can see God. Beatrice, the woman Dante loved, and all the saints join the prayer. Mary lifts her eyes to the light.

Dante looks up, and his sight goes deeper into the light of God. What he sees is more than words or memory can hold, like a dream that leaves only its feeling behind.

In the depths of the light, everything scattered through the universe is bound together by love, like pages in one book. Then he sees three circles of three colors and one size. Inside one of them is a human form.

He cannot understand how that form fits the circle. Then a flash strikes his mind and grants his wish. His strength fails, but his desire and will now turn like a wheel, moved by the love that moves the sun and the stars.
